title: Lamar's — Counter Cheat Sheets: Spotting Fakes
law: Selling or offering goods under a counterfeit trademark, knowing it, is a crime in Florida (§831.032). It is a felony at 100 items or $2,500 of retail value.
front: Lamar's — Counter Cheat Sheets: Spotting Fakes
Current as of September 20, 2026 · Keep at the counter · Testing steps and the test kit are in the binder (Tabs 5 and 6)
These sheets catch the common fakes, not the expert ones. When a check fails or you are not sure, price only what you can prove, or pass. Sheet 1 applies to everything.
| 1 | Ground rules for anything with a big name on it |
| 3 | Gold and silver coins and bars (bullion) |
| 8 | Red dots, holographic sights and scopes |

sheets.title: Ground rules for anything with a big name on it
intro: Brand names are what fakers copy, and a fake costs whatever was paid for it. These rules apply to every sheet that follows.

sections.heading: 60-second check
body: The name is not the collateral until it is proven. Price what you can verify today: the metal, the weight, a cert that matches. Everything else is a no-name item.
Ask where it came from and how long he has had it. A real owner answers easily. Write the answer on the ticket.
Check the price against the market. "New" at half price is the most common tell on every sheet.
Run the sheet for that item. Use the free lookup it lists, and type the number in yourself.

sections.heading: Full check
body: Never scan a QR code or follow a link printed on a holder, card or tag. Fake slabs and cards point to copycat sites. Type the maker's address yourself.
A matching serial number is not proof. Fakers copy real serials and cert numbers. The item in hand has to match the lookup photo and details.
Boxes, papers, certificates and receipts are faked too. They support a real item; they never make a doubtful one real.
Photograph the marks, serials and labels, tie the photos to the ticket, and write down what was checked (binder Tab 6).
Several of the same brand-name item from one seller, especially new in the box, means stop.

sections.heading: Fakes give themselves away by
body: A price that is too good, "no returns," or a seller in a hurry
A story that changes, or no story at all
Blurry print, misspellings, crooked logos, light weight, cheap hardware
Myth: "It came with a certificate." Anyone can print one.

sections.heading: Look it up free
body: | Item | Where | Sheet |
| Graded coins | ngccoin.com/certlookup · pcgs.com/cert | 3 |
| Diamond reports | GIA Report Check (gia.edu) · IGI · GCAL | 4 |
| Graded cards | psacard.com/cert · Beckett · SGC · CGC | 6 |
| Autographs | PSA/DNA · JSA · Beckett · MLB · Fanatics | 7 |
| Optics | Trijicon serial lookup · call Leupold, Aimpoint, EOTech | 8 |
| Apple | checkcoverage.apple.com · Parts and Service History | 10 |

sections.heading: Still not sure?
body: Lend or buy on what you can prove (the metal, a no-name value), or pass. A lost sale costs nothing; a fake costs the whole loan.

Never sell a known fake as the real brand. Selling or offering goods with a counterfeit trademark, knowing it, is a crime in Florida (§831.032): a misdemeanor, and a felony at 100 items or $2,500 of retail value. Federal law (18 U.S.C. §2320) covers it too.

sheets.rule: a fake found after intake is set aside, never tagged for the floor under the brand name, and handled as the pawn rules require for that ticket.
sheets.sources: [Fla. Stat. §831.032, counterfeit trademarks](http://www.leg.state.fl.us/statutes/index.cfm?App_mode=Display_Statute&URL=0800-0899/0831/Sections/0831.032.html) · The sources on sheets 2–11

sheets.title: Gold and silver jewelry
intro: Fakes are plated base metal, sometimes tungsten, stamped 14K, 18K or 925. We pay by metal weight, so a fake costs everything paid.

sections.heading: 60-second check
body: The testing steps in the binder (Tab 6), short version:
Weigh it in grams.
Loupe the stamp for a karat or 925 mark plus a maker's mark. US law requires both, so a missing one is a warning sign.
Magnet: if the piece is pulled (not just the clasp spring), no gold price.
File a notch and put acid in the notch. Plating passes a surface test.

sections.heading: Full check
body: If the acid reads lower than the stamp, quote the lower karat.
Test several links or beads. Fake bead necklaces passed magnet and acid at several pawn shops.
Hollow chains and hoops are light. Pay on weight only.
On 925, use silver acid in a notch. Red or light brown means sterling, green means not silver, and cream means plated (check your kit's chart).
Real brand marks:
James Avery: "925" and "sterling" (before 2004, "sterling" only). Gold is "14K" or "585". Its bronze and steel pieces aren't precious.
Tiffany: "Tiffany & Co." or "T & Co", with "925" or "AG925" on silver and "750" on gold. Links are soldered, with no join line.
Pandora: "ALE" plus "S925", "G585" or "G750". Gold-colored Pandora without G585 or G750 is plated.
David Yurman: "D.Y." or "David Yurman" with a crisp ©, plus "925". The cable (twisted rope) is tight and evenly darkened.
Specs to check against
| Stamp | Means | Pay for it? |
| 10K / 417 | 10 karat | Yes, after acid |
| 14K / 585 | 14 karat | Yes, after acid |
| 18K / 750 | 18 karat | Yes, after acid |
| 22K / 916 | 22 karat | Yes, after acid |
| 375 | 9 karat (Europe) | As 9K, after acid |
| 925, S925, AG925 | Sterling silver | Silver only |
| GF, 1/20 12K | Gold filled: gold layer is 1/20 of weight | No |
| GP, GE, 18KGE, HGE, RGP | Plated. In 18KGE, only the skin is 18K | No |

sections.heading: Fakes give themselves away by
body: Brassy, pink or gray metal showing at the clasp, edges or inside a ring.
A crooked, shallow or blurry stamp, or misspelled brand engraving.
A brand piece priced far under retail, or sold "new" by an unofficial website. The box proves nothing.
Yurman fakes: light, wrong width, crooked gold wrap, glass stones.

Myths: "It's heavy, so it's real" (tungsten weighs about the same as gold). "The magnet didn't stick" (brass doesn't either). "It's stamped 14K" (stamps are easy to fake). The bite test proves nothing.

sections.heading: Look it up free
body: No serial lookup exists, and Tiffany doesn't authenticate. Compare the design on jamesavery.com ("Designs From Our Archives"), tiffany.com, pandora.net or davidyurman.com.

sections.heading: Still not sure?
body: Lend or buy on the metal only, at the lower karat, or pass.
Don't use the Sigma verifier on jewelry. Only XRF sees through plating every time.

sheets.rule: pay nothing extra for a brand name, and no notch allowed means no deal.

sheets.title: Gold and silver coins and bars (bullion)
intro: Chinese fakers copy Eagles, Morgans and bars, and even the grading holders. We pay close to melt, so one fake costs nearly everything paid.

sections.heading: 60-second check
body: Weigh it in grams and check the table. Fakes are often a little off. A 1 oz Gold Eagle or Krugerrand weighs about 33.93 g, not 31.1 g, because it is 22K alloy.
Calipers: diameter against the table, thickness against a coin you know is real.
Magnet: nothing should stick. On silver, do the slide test: tilt the piece about 45 degrees and set the magnet on it. On real silver it slides down slowly instead of sticking.

Sigma verifier, if the store buys one (coins and bars only, from $999): set the metal and size, then test both sides. It reads through flips, slabs and assay cards. Without one, lean harder on weight, calipers and the slab lookup.
Loupe the date and mint mark (the small letter for the mint that made it). Check that the pair exists (see "Dates that exist").

sections.heading: Full check
body: Slabs (sealed NGC or PCGS holders): type the cert number into the official site yourself and compare the coin with the photos. Never scan a QR code on the slab, because fake slabs link to copycat sites.
Assay cards (the sealed card a bar comes in): the serial number on the bar must match the card. Cards get faked too.
Gold bars: tungsten weighs almost the same as gold, so a gold-plated tungsten bar can pass weight and size. The Sigma's Bullion wand finds tungsten up to 1.5 mm under gold, not deeper.
Ping test: tap the coin lightly. Real coins ring, and many cast fakes don't. It takes practice or an app such as Pingcoin, and it only supports other tests.
Junk silver (90% silver coins dated 1964 or earlier): weigh each coin. Copper-nickel clad coins show a copper stripe on the edge. Kennedy halves from 1965 to 1970 are 40% silver.
Security features: recent Maple Leafs have fine radial lines and a tiny engraved leaf with the year's last two digits (loupe). Eagles from 2021 on have a special pattern in the edge ridges.
Bars and 1 oz rounds: check the maker's name, the weight and ".999". One troy ounce is 31.103 g, so a 10 oz bar is 311.03 g.
Dates that exist

Old 90% Morgan dollars: 1878–1904 and 1921 only. "D" appears only in 1921, and "CC" only in 1878–1885 and 1889–1893. An 1895 with no mint mark was made only as a proof, so treat one as fake unless it is in a verified slab.
Old 90% Peace dollars: 1921–1928 and 1934–1935 only.
Since 2021 the US Mint has made new 99.9% silver Morgans and Peace dollars (including a "D"). These are real.
Gold and Silver Eagles: 1986 and later.
Specs to check against
| Coin | Metal | Weight (g) | Diameter (mm) | Thickness (mm)\* |
| Silver Maple Leaf, 1 oz | 99.99% silver | 31.11 | 38 | \_\_\_\_ |
| Morgan or Peace dollar | 90% silver | 26.73 | 38.1 | \_\_\_\_ |
\*The mints don't publish thickness for these coins. Measure a coin you know is real and write the number in. Worn old coins can weigh a little under the table.

sections.heading: Fakes give themselves away by
body: Wrong weight or size, or a magnet that sticks. NGC found a fake 1895-O Morgan at 25.87 g, almost a gram light, made of copper, zinc and nickel.
Soft, mushy detail, grainy or pimpled surfaces, or the same tiny dent in the same spot on every coin from a fake die.
A seam around the edge, tool marks near the date or mint mark, or heavy fake toning (coloring).
A date and mint mark combination that was never made.
Slabs with crooked label text, a barcode that won't scan, or a QR code that leads anywhere but ngccoin.com or pcgs.com.
A price well under melt, or "no returns."

Myths: "It's heavy, so it's real" (tungsten weighs nearly the same as gold). "The magnet didn't stick, so it's silver" (brass and aluminum don't stick either). "It's in a slab or assay card" (both get faked).

sections.heading: Look it up free
body: NGC Cert Lookup: ngccoin.com/certlookup. Enter the cert number and grade. Most coins graded since 2008 have photos.
PCGS Cert Verification: pcgs.com/cert, or the free PCGS app (barcode scan or NFC tap). NGC also has a free app.
PAMP Veriscan app: scan a Veriscan-marked PAMP bar.
PCGS CoinFacts (pcgs.com/coinfacts): check that a date and mint mark exist.

sections.heading: Still not sure?
body: If weight, size and magnet pass (and the Sigma, if there is one), pay the bullion price. If any one fails, pass.
On an odd Sigma reading, recalibrate, test another spot and compare with a known-real coin.

sheets.rule: buy gold bars over 1 oz only after an outside test. Even a Sigma can't see a deep tungsten core.

sheets.title: Diamonds and gemstones
intro: A claimed diamond may be moissanite (a lab-made look-alike), cubic zirconia (CZ), glass, white sapphire or lab-grown (real diamond, factory-made); Lamar's does not pay for stones, but know what you hold.

sections.heading: 60-second check
body: Say the rule first: we pay on the metal; the stone rides free.

Multi-tester (reads heat and electrical flow). Stone clean, dry, room temperature. Fingers on the tester's metal grips. Tip square to the table (big top facet), firm pressure. Loose stone: set it on the metal rest and hold the rest.
Diamond: natural or lab-grown. It cannot tell them apart.
Moissanite: moissanite, the tip touched metal, or rarely a lab-grown diamond. Retest.
Neither: CZ, glass, white sapphire or similar.
Loupe the band. "CZ" stamped means cubic zirconia. A stone set in silver (925, STER) is usually an imitation. Metal is a clue, not proof.

sections.heading: Full check
body: Tester care. Presidium testers are factory-calibrated; nothing to adjust (other brands: follow the manual). Weak batteries give false readings. Suggested rule: test a known CZ and moissanite at opening.
Loupe the stone at an angle through the side. Moissanite shows doubled facet edges. Glass and CZ show rounded, chipped or worn edges and round bubbles. A flawless look proves nothing.

Report. Look up the number (below), then find it laser-written on the girdle (the thin outer edge) and match it and the weight. GIA marks lab-grown "Laboratory-Grown"; IGI puts "LG" before the number. Fake inscriptions exist.
Lab-grown needs a screening machine, such as the GIA iD100 ($5,795). Not worth it here. Resale is poor: wholesale prices fell an average 26% in 2025, and most big diamond buyers take natural only.
Colored stones in class rings and older jewelry are often lab-made or glass. At 10x, curved growth lines or round bubbles mean synthetic ruby or sapphire; bubbles also mean glass.

sections.heading: Fakes give themselves away by
body: Doubled facet edges.
"CZ" in the band; a big stone in silver or plated metal.
Bubbles; rounded or scratched facet edges.
Report number or weight that doesn't match.
Myth: the fog test. Results are inconsistent, and moissanite clears fast too.
Myth: "It scratches glass." Moissanite and sapphire do too, and it can damage the stone.
Myth: reading print through it. It depends on the cut; never definitive.
Myth: "It sparkles." CZ and moissanite sparkle.

sections.heading: Look it up free
body: GIA Report Check at gia.edu
IGI Verify Your Report at igi.org
Verify Your GCAL Certificate at gcalusa.com

sections.heading: Still not sure?
body: Price the metal only: weigh whole, take 15% off.
Single stone over about a carat: don't estimate. Offer to pull it, or send him to a jeweler.
Wants money for the stone: send him to a jeweler.

sheets.title: Rolex and luxury watches
intro: Fake Rolexes are common, the best ("superclones") pass most counter checks, and one bad loan costs thousands.

sections.heading: 60-second check
body: Seconds hand. A modern Rolex sweeps in small, fast steps. One tick a second means quartz: fake, unless a real Oysterquartz.
Back. Most models: solid and plain. A clear back is rare (the 1908 has one).
Cyclops (magnifying bubble over the date): date fills it, dead center. Small or off-center date means fake.
Loupe the dial. Printing crisp and slightly raised, markers straight. Fuzzy or crooked: fake.

sections.heading: Full check
body: Numbers. Reference (model) number between the lugs at 12, behind the bracelet. Serial between the lugs at 6 (older) or on the rehaut, the inner ring around the dial, which also reads "ROLEX" all around (newer). Deep, sharp, and matching the papers.
Crown in the crystal at 6 o'clock: tiny dots, seen only at 10x in angled light. A thick frosted line means fake.
Lume: modern models glow blue (Chromalight).
Clasp: crown and stamps crisp; solid links, heavy for its size.
Other brands:
Omega: "Master Chronometer" on the dial? Omega says a magnet held near stops a fake, not a real one. Don't magnet other watches.
TAG Heuer: model and serial engraved on the back; press the pushers, and the chronograph subdials must work.
Breitling: made since October 2020? It has a digital passport; ask to see it.
Cartier: tiny "Cartier" hidden in the VII or X on most models since the 1990s. Fakes copy it; check it is sharp.
Specs to check against
| Check | Genuine Rolex |
| Seconds hand | 28,800 beats/hour = 8 steps a second (most modern); Land-Dweller (2025): 10; Oysterquartz (about 1977–2001): 1 |
| Serial on rehaut | From 2005; only there from 2008 |
| Random serials | From about 2010–2011 |
| Crystal crown | Phased in 1999 to early 2004 |
| Cyclops | Dealers cite 2.5x; Rolex no longer publishes a figure |

sections.heading: Fakes give themselves away by
body: One-second tick; clear back; small or off-center date.
Shallow engraving, fuzzy print, light bracelet.
Myth: "It has the box and papers." Both are faked.
Myth: "The hand sweeps, so it's real." Good fakes sweep too.

sections.heading: Look it up free
body: rolex.com: the model's photos; locator for Official Rolex Jewelers.
Omega Master Chronometer: certificate number at omegawatches.com.
Breitling digital passport: in the owner's Breitling account.

sections.heading: Still not sure?
body: Superclones beat most checks above. For a big loan, have a watchmaker open the back and check the movement (AWCI "Find a Professional", search by zip), or ask an Official Rolex Jeweler about a Rolex inspection (about $150, per one dealer).

sheets.rule: lend nothing on the brand name until a watchmaker has opened it; lend as on a no-name watch, or pass.

sheets.title: Sports cards and Pokémon cards
intro: Graded cases, vintage stars, modern autograph cards and Pokémon cards are all faked, and even a real card's price depends on its condition.

sections.heading: 60-second check
body: Slab (sealed grading case): enter the cert number in the grader's free lookup. Card, year and grade must match the label.
The lookup photo must match the card in hand: centering, print specks, corner nicks. Fakers reuse real cert numbers. Older certs may lack photos.
Squeeze the case. Real ones are stiff; flex, cloudy seams, cracks or glue mean it was opened.
Raw (ungraded) vintage card: under the loupe, real post-war cards show a crisp rosette (a honeycomb of color dots). Blurry, muddy or pixel-like dots mean a copy.

sections.heading: Full check
body: PSA label: held to a light, the back's print should show through (a glued-on fake front blocks it). On newer labels, front and back cert numbers match and the logo flicks on and off as you tilt.
"Authentic Altered" on a label means trimmed or recolored: value it low.
Vintage: measure with calipers (table). One edge whiter or slicker than the rest, or razor-sharp corners, suggests trimming. Pre-war cards print soft; a neat dot grid on one is a warning.

Modern: forgers peel a sticker autograph off a cheap card and forge a star's name. A multi-color patch on a /99 card is suspect; lifted edges or glue mean a swap. The set checklist should show it signed and numbered that way.

Pokémon: beside a real card from the same set, check fonts, energy symbols, back blue (fakes run light or purplish) and holo (flat on fakes). A phone light shines through fakes more. The rip test shows a black middle layer but destroys the card; use it only on your own cheap card.
Condition (centering, corners, edges, surface) sets the price, so a raw card's value is a guess.
Specs to check against
| Card | Size, inches |
| 1957 Topps onward; Pokémon | 2-1/2 × 3-1/2 |

sections.heading: Fakes give themselves away by
body: A dull, grayish label, off fonts or a blurry hologram
Thin, glossy stock or dyed tan edges
Myth: "It's in a PSA case, so it's real." Cases are faked.
Myth: "It looks old." Reprints are aged on purpose.

sections.heading: Look it up free
body: PSA: psacard.com/cert (type the number in; don't trust a QR code on a slab)
BGS: beckett.com/grading/card-lookup
SGC: gosgc.com or the SGC Grading app (photos)
CGC: cgccards.com/certlookup (photos)
Pokémon: pokemon.com/us/pokemon-tcg/pokemon-cards (check name, HP, attacks)

sections.heading: Still not sure?
body: Otherwise, grade it first: PSA starts at about $60 a card and takes 90–100 business days.
Good fakes need an expert. If unsure, pass.

sheets.rule: lend only on cards graded by PSA, BGS, SGC or CGC whose cert and photo match the card.

sheets.title: Autographs and memorabilia
intro: Signed balls, photos, jerseys and "game-used" gear are forged in bulk, often with printed certificates to match, and a fake signature leaves an item worth only what it would be unsigned.

sections.heading: 60-second check
body: Find the authenticator's sticker or hologram and its matching card or letter. Only five count: PSA/DNA, JSA, Beckett (BAS), MLB Authentication and Fanatics.
Look up the number free (below). The signer and the kind of item (ball, bat, photo, jersey) must match. A real number from another item means a fake.
A sticker that looks peeled, cut, lifted or reprinted fails. Real PSA/DNA stickers break apart if moved (older ones show a checkerboard). MLB holograms show tampering if removed.
None of the five? Value it as unsigned.

sections.heading: Full check
body: A store's or seller's own COA (certificate of authenticity), a "lifetime guarantee" or a photo of the signing proves nothing. Forgers print their own.
A "PSA/DNA QuickOpinion: likely genuine" email is a $10 opinion from photos, not a cert.
Autopen (signing machine): the line keeps the same width and pressure at a steady speed, with blunt starts and stops or tiny ink blobs, and sometimes a slight shake. Real signing tapers and flows.

Printed (facsimile) signature on a photo or ball: tilt it under a light, and real ink shines differently. A printed one shows the photo's dots under the loupe, sits flat, and leaves no pen groove. Two identical signatures mean printed or machine-signed.
Some signatures were stamped, or signed by a secretary or clubhouse attendant. Only an authenticator can call these.

"Game-used" needs an MLB hologram whose lookup says game-used, or a photo-match letter from PSA or MeiGray (the item matched to game photos by its stains, repairs and tags). "Team Issued" does not mean game-used.
Most-forged names (PSA, 2025): Mantle, Jordan, DiMaggio, Kobe Bryant, Ted Williams, Babe Ruth, Ohtani, Donald Trump, Willie Mays and Muhammad Ali.

sections.heading: Fakes give themselves away by
body: A sticker number that doesn't match its card or letter
A star's name, a low price and the seller's own COA
Myth: "It comes with a COA." Anyone can print one.
Myth: "It has a hologram." Only one you can look up counts.

sections.heading: Look it up free
body: PSA/DNA: psacard.com/cert (often text only, so check the signer and item)
JSA: spenceloa.com, Verify Authenticity page
Beckett (BAS): beckett-authentication.com
MLB: mlb.com/authentication (two letters, the number, and the validation code if there is one)
Fanatics: fanatics.com/fansecure (two letters and the number, e.g. CV123456; type it in rather than scanning a code)

sections.heading: Still not sure?
body: The customer can get it certified by PSA/DNA, JSA or Beckett and come back.
PSA will review a PSA-certified item if you contact them before buying.

sheets.rule: value anything without a real third-party cert (one of the five, matching on lookup) as if unsigned.

sheets.title: Red dots, holographic sights and scopes
intro: Airsoft copies of EOTech, Aimpoint, Trijicon and big-name scopes look right on a rifle, and a loan on one is a total loss.

sections.heading: 60-second check
body: Dot color. Aimpoint: red only. EOTech: red or green, never switchable. A red/green switch means fake.
Front glass. EOTech: flat and dark; fakes are curved and mirror the room lights. Aimpoint: looks red (maybe orange or green), never blue or clear. A visible LED inside means fake.
Serial. Aimpoint: engraved on the side, same as the box. EOTech: sticker on the bottom. Missing or crude means fake.
Battery. EOTech takes only CR123, AA or N cell. Hearing-aid button cells, or a solar panel on an "Aimpoint," mean fake.

sections.heading: Full check
body: "Made in." Aimpoint: Sweden only. Leupold riflescopes: Oregon only. EOTech HWS, Trijicon RMR: USA. Vortex is made in several countries including China, so "China" proves nothing there.
EOTech NV button dims the reticle almost to nothing (for night vision goggles). On fakes it changes color.
EOTech window. EOTech says a real one keeps working with the window partly blocked. Cover half the front glass with a card: the reticle should still show.
ACOG (TA31 type): no battery; tritium and fiber optic light it, so the reticle glows in a dark room. Tritium fades by half about every 12 years: old means dim, not fake.
Leupold: Leupold medallion (logo emblem) always present; serial and barcode on the bottom.
Thermal and night vision (Pulsar, AGM, ATN, iRayUSA): housing serial matches the menu. Never ship or sell one abroad: ATN says that is unlawful without a license.
Specs to check against
| Sight | Weight | Battery | Made in | New, maker's site |
| EOTech EXPS3 | 11.2 oz | 1 CR123 | USA | $859 |
| EOTech 512 | 11.5 oz | 2 AA | USA | $569 |
| Aimpoint Micro T-2 | 3.3 oz, sight only | CR2032 | Sweden | $951 |
| Aimpoint PRO | 6.8 oz, sight only | DL1/3N | Sweden | $479 |
| Trijicon RMR Type 2 (LED) | 1.17 oz | CR2032 | USA | — |

sections.heading: Fakes give themselves away by
body: Strong blue, gray or muddy tint; price far under the table.
Leupold Mark 4 with silver lettering; Prismatic with no serial; several scopes sharing one serial.
Myth: "It has a serial sticker, so it's real." EOTech says fakes copy the stickers.

sections.heading: Look it up free
body: Trijicon Serial Number Lookup (trijicon.com): says whether Trijicon made that serial; not a guarantee.
Leupold: call 1-800-LEUPOLD with the serial and ask if it is authentic.
Aimpoint: serial tool at aimpoint.us (sign-in), or (703) 263-9795, option 6.
Pulsar: email the serial to support@pulsar-vision.com; they verify it.
No online check found: call EOTech (734) 356-8030, Vortex 1-800-4VORTEX, Nightforce (208) 476-9814 ext. 3.

sections.heading: Still not sure?
body: Trijicon calls any used Trijicon "buyer beware": fakes and stolen goods. The serial on the state form covers stolen. Good fakes pass counter checks.

sheets.rule: no loan on the brand until the maker has checked the serial; otherwise lend as a no-name optic, or pass.

sheets.title: Power tool batteries and tools
intro: Counterfeit Milwaukee M18, DeWalt 20V, Makita 18V and Ryobi ONE+ packs sell cheap online, hold far less than the label says, and can catch fire.

sections.heading: 60-second check
body: Labels. Blurry, off-center, peeling or misspelled print, or commas in web addresses (DeWalt), mean fake.
Screws (DeWalt): genuine are silver and domed; fakes are flatter with a black coating.
Makita: black; logo and "Lithium-Ion" on both sides; logo and a white plug on the bottom; a red stripe inside the pressed latch.
Ryobi: the R and B in "RYOBI" have indents; model, serial and safety marks printed on it.
Fuel gauge (Milwaukee): genuine lights step up one by one; a fake lights all at once, dimmer.

sections.heading: Full check
body: Weigh it and look up the model number. Lighter than the table is a hint, not proof. DeWalt says fakes carry part numbers that don't exist.

Load test (binder Tab 6): run it down and read the amp-hours. In Project Farm's test, genuine 5Ah packs gave 93% of their rating; fakes 47–70%. Worn genuine packs test low too: price on the test, not the label.
Charger must charge it.
Pack already open? Don't open one for a customer. Fakes show one layer of cells and polystyrene filler where genuine Makita has two layers; small cells (1,500–2,000 mAh where 2,500 belongs).
"Compatible" packs ("for Milwaukee") aren't counterfeit, just no-name: price them that way.
Snap-on hand tools: name and part number stamped crisp (fakes stamped "Snap-en" have turned up). No "USA" stamp alone isn't a tell. Blue-Point is Snap-on's cheaper line.
Specs to check against
| 5Ah pack (Project Farm test) | Genuine weight | Fake weight | Genuine tested | Fake tested |
| Milwaukee M18 | 724 g | 634 g | 84 Wh (about 4.7 Ah) | 42 Wh (about 2.4 Ah) |
| DeWalt 20V | 646 g | 612 g | 84 Wh | 63 Wh (about 3.5 Ah) |
| Makita 18V LXT | 646 g (Makita lists 0.63 kg) | 555 g | 84 Wh | 47 Wh (about 2.6 Ah) |
All rated 90 Wh; tested at a steady 7 amps. Amp-hours = watt-hours ÷ 18.

sections.heading: Fakes give themselves away by
body: "New" at half price: the fakes cost $42–48 against $70–82 genuine.
A big amp-hour label that tests small.
Myth: "It's heavy, so it's real." Fakes were only 34–91 g lighter.
Myth: "Four bars, so it's good." The gauge shows charge, not capacity.

sections.heading: Look it up free
body: Milwaukee 1-800-729-3878: warranty runs on the date code; no registration needed.
DeWalt 800-433-9258: ask whether the part number is real.
Makita (800) 4-MAKITA.

sections.heading: Still not sure?
body: Makita warns fakes can burst or catch fire. Never charge a suspect pack unattended.

sheets.rule: a pack with fake tells gets $0 and goes back to the customer, never onto the shelf (the Power Tool Institute calls counterfeits illegal). Every other pack is priced on its load test.

sheets.title: Apple and electronics
intro: Fake AirPods, Apple Watches and Beats look right in the box, and a used iPhone can hide non-Apple parts.

sections.heading: 60-second check
body: Serial in Settings = serial on the item = serial on the box. Where to look: table below.
Apple Check Coverage (checkcoverage.apple.com): type the serial and the code shown; no sign-in needed. No record means pass.
AirPods: connect them to an iPhone. A "Cannot Verify AirPods" alert ("could not be verified as genuine") means fake.

sections.heading: Full check
body: AirPods: open Settings, tap the AirPods name. Model, firmware and serial should all show; blank or nonsense firmware means fake. Noise-cancelling models show Noise Control. AirPods 2 and later and AirPods Pro 1 and 2 have a serial on each earbud; clones often reuse one serial for both.

iPhone: Settings \> General \> About \> Parts and Service History (iOS 15.2 and later). "Unknown" means not a genuine Apple part or not working; "Used" means taken from another iPhone. iPhone 12 and later list battery, display, cameras and logic board; iPhone 11 battery and display. IMEI from \*\#06\# must match Settings and the SIM tray (iPhone 6s–13).

Apple Watch: Apple's buyer check: pair it to an iPhone with the Watch app. If it asks for the last owner's Apple Account, Activation Lock is still on. Knockoffs run a generic system with no App Store and a non-Apple charger.
Beats: Settings, tap the Beats name. On earbuds, tap the serial to see left, then right.
AirPods box: several small labels, not one big sticker; manual, safety sheet and warranty card inside.
Specs to check against
| Item | Serial in software | Serial on the item |
| iPhone | Settings \> General \> About (serial and IMEI) | IMEI on SIM tray (6s–13); both on box barcode |
| AirPods, AirPods Pro | Settings \> AirPods name | Under the case lid |
| AirPods Max | Settings \> AirPods name | Under the left ear cushion |
| Apple Watch | Watch: Settings \> General \> About | Inside the band slot |
| Beats | Settings \> Beats name | Headband slider (Solo 4, Studio Pro); inside the case (earbuds) |

sections.heading: Fakes give themselves away by
body: Box, case and Settings serials that don't match.
Missing Noise Control or Find My features; firmware that never updates.
Blue LED on the case, loose hinge, rough seams.
Myth: "Check Coverage found it, so it's real." Most cloned AirPods use a real serial.

sections.heading: Look it up free
body: Apple Check Coverage (checkcoverage.apple.com): serial and code.
Parts and Service History: on the iPhone itself.
stolenphonechecker.org: IMEI blacklist (store rule).

sections.heading: Still not sure?
body: Phones: buy, never lend (store rule): IMEI check, he turns off Find My, reset, Hello screen. Apple: an "iPhone Locked to Owner" screen means don't take it.
Fails any check: pass. Good clones pass counter checks; on earbuds, when in doubt, pass.

sheets.rule: Apple Watch follows the phone rule: buy only; he unpairs it at the counter, then it must pair fresh.

sheets.title: Other things that get faked
intro: YETI, Oakley, Ray-Ban, designer bags, Jordans and premium knives are copied well enough to pass a glance; these checks catch only lazy fakes.

sections.heading: 60-second check
body: Price. "New" at a big discount is the top tell. Chris Reeve never discounts, Louis Vuitton rarely does, and Ray-Ban's owner sets minimum advertised prices.
Print and spelling. Logos crisp, words spelled right. A misspelling means fake.
Maker's marks where they belong (below). Missing is a warning sign.

sections.heading: Full check
body: YETI coolers and tumblers
Hard coolers and drinkware: serial or QR code on the bottom. Soft coolers: a tag on the outside.
YETI's warranty covers only gear bought from YETI or an authorized dealer: ask where it came from.
Oakley and Ray-Ban
Ray-Ban describes its lens marks as etched: "RB" on the left lens, full signature on the right (custom lenses). Look for crisp etching; printed or missing means doubt.
Oakley publishes no checklist; send photos (below).
Designer handbags (Louis Vuitton, Coach, Michael Kors)
Louis Vuitton: older bags have a small inside tab with two letters and some numbers (date code). Newer bags use a chip instead, so a date code on a 2022-or-later model is a red flag.
Stitches short, dense and even. Heat stamp (pressed-in logo) centered and deep. Hardware engraving sharp. Thin, shallow or faint means fake.
Coach and Michael Kors: no maker check found.
Nike Air Jordan 1
Tag inside the tongue: clean print. Wavy or misaligned means fake.
From behind, the heel curves in and out like an hourglass; fakes are straight.
Toe-box holes clean and even; Wings logo letters thin, not touching.
Box label: normal-weight font; fakes print bolder.
Premium knives
Chris Reeve: fakes show wrong materials, rough machining marks, misspellings.
Spyderco: some fakes are "frighteningly accurate."
Benchmade: no maker guide found.

sections.heading: Fakes give themselves away by
body: Blurry logos, long thin stitches, faint hardware engraving.
Myth: "It has a date code, so it's a real LV." Fakes print date codes, and newer real bags have none.

sections.heading: Look it up free
body: YETI: "Register Your Gear" on yeti.com takes the serial; store locator lists authorized dealers.
Oakley: email Customer Care (oakley.com) clear photos and where it was bought; Oakley says it will tell you if it's real. Phone 1-800-403-7449.
Chris Reeve: Authorized Dealers list on chrisreeve.com, or call (208) 375-0367 to verify.
Spyderco: dealer locator; post photos on forum.spyderco.com; 1-800-525-7770.
Benchmade: dealer locator on benchmade.com; 1-833-557-2526.

sections.heading: Still not sure?
body: Legit Check (legitcheck.app): from $10; 30 minutes to 48 hours.
Real Authentication (realauthentication.com): $30, answer within 24 hours.
Entrupy (phone app): business plans from $139 a month; only worth it at volume.
Anything else that fails a check: lend as no-name, or pass.
